items.content:
U.S. Stock Futures Point Higher as AI Developments and Earnings Support Market Recovery: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Nasdaq sign on building ©ajay_suresh U.S. stock futures indicated a higher opening on Tuesday, suggesting Wall Street could extend Monday's gains as investors assessed developments in artificial intelligence, quarterly corporate earnings and the outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy.
Renewed attention to AI-related companies followed Anthropic's public filing for an initial public offering and an expanded partnership between Nvidia and Meta Platforms.
Corporate earnings also influenced premarket trading, with JetBlue Airways and Corning advancing, while Whirlpool declined following disappointing quarterly results and a reduction in its annual revenue guidance.
Investors were also preparing for Wednesday's Federal Reserve policy announcement, with interest rates widely expected to remain unchanged.
Artificial Intelligence Developments Support U.S. Equity Futures
AI-related developments remained a focus for investors following recent volatility in technology shares.
Anthropic's public filing for an initial public offering contributed to renewed interest in the sector, following concerns about the financing requirements associated with large-scale AI infrastructure investment.
Those concerns had weighed on U.S. equities late in the previous week, particularly as investors assessed the implications of debt-financed spending on computing capacity and related infrastructure.
Attention also turned to an expanded collaboration between Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META).
The companies announced plans to broaden their work on Muse and the Muse family of artificial intelligence models.
As part of the arrangement, Nvidia said it would invest $3 billion in Meta, which is pursuing plans to raise up to $95 billion through equity financing.
The announcements provided additional developments for investors assessing spending and commercial activity across the AI industry.
JetBlue and Corning Advance Following Quarterly Earnings
Several companies recorded notable premarket movements following their latest financial announcements.
JetBlue Airways (NASDAQ:JBLU) shares climbed 13.9% before the opening bell, despite the airline reporting a third-quarter loss larger than analysts had anticipated.
The company also indicated that it expects further operating margin expansion during the fourth quarter.
Corning (NYSE:GLW) shares advanced in premarket trading after the glass manufacturer reported third-quarter revenue and earnings above Wall Street estimates.
The results contributed to company-specific share price movements ahead of the regular trading session.
Whirlpool Declines After Lowering Annual Revenue Guidance
Whirlpool (NYSE:WHR) shares fell 7.2% in premarket trading after the appliance manufacturer reported third-quarter financial results below analyst expectations.
The company also reduced its full-year revenue guidance.
The announcement added to investor attention on corporate profitability and demand conditions across consumer-related industries.
Whirlpool's decline contrasted with the premarket advances recorded by JetBlue and Corning, reflecting different responses to the latest earnings announcements.
The Federal Reserve's upcoming monetary policy announcement remained a central consideration for financial markets.
The central bank is scheduled to announce its interest rate decision on Wednesday, with market participants widely expecting policymakers to maintain current borrowing costs.
Investors will also examine the accompanying policy statement for indications of how officials assess inflation, economic activity and the future direction of interest rates.
The pending decision could contribute to restrained trading activity ahead of the announcement.
Wall Street Rebounds Following Previous Week's Declines
U.S. equities recovered on Monday after recording losses during the final two sessions of the previous week.
The Nasdaq Composite advanced 214.04 points, or 0.8%, to close at 26,169.38.

items.summary: Trump’s oil and gas investments have doubled since the Iran war  The Independent
items.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
President Donald Trump’s personal holdings in oil and gas stocks nearly doubled in value in the past year while regular Americans have experienced soaring fuel prices from the Iran war, a new report revealed.
Trump’s holdings in those stocks are worth between $22.5 million and $81.6 million, up from between $12.6 million and $46 million at the end of 2025, Democrats on the congressional Joint Economic Committee announced in a report Monday.
The increase reflects both rising values in stocks Trump already owned and millions of dollars in new purchases this year. More than 94 percent of those purchases came after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, the report said.
Americans have faced sharply higher fuel costs as a result of the conflict, which has stretched on for seven months with no clear end in sight. The national average price of gasoline stood at $4.29 a gallon Monday, up from $2.98 two days before the conflict began, according to AAA . American families have spent an additional $101 billion on gas since the war began — an average of $856 per family, the report found.
Trump has repeatedly called higher oil prices a “ small price to pay ” for neutralizing Iran’s nuclear threat, even as polls show those costs remain a source of anxiety for many voters. At a rally Saturday, the president touted the profits flowing to American oil companies, telling supporters: “We’re making a freakin’ fortune.”
President Donald Trump’s personal holdings in gas and oil stocks have nearly doubled since 2025, according to a new report ( Getty )
“The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars,” Trump said. “Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what's happened in the Middle East.”
ExxonMobil and Chevron account for most of Trump’s oil and gas holdings. Both companies’ shares have climbed more than 20 percent since February.
The White House said the 80-year-old president remains focused on easing pain at the pump and has no direct role in managing his stock portfolio.
“President Trump’s priority has been and continues to be lowering gas prices for American families,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told The Independent . “The President’s stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000.”
The national average price of gasoline stood at $4.29 a gallon Monday, up from $2.98 two days before the conflict began, according to AAA. Pictured: a gas station in Georgia on October 23 ( Reuters )
“Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle added. “All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest.”
Trump, the nation’s wealthiest president, has seen his net worth rise by more than $1 billion since returning to office last year, driven largely by his cryptocurrency and hospitality investments.
The report’s findings come a week ahead of the midterm elections , with multiple polls predicting heavy Republican losses that could cost the party control of both the House and the Senate.

items.title: Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision again over Israel participation
items.summary: A Dutch broadcaster reverses a decision to take part, citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation.
items.content:
Image caption, Claude Kiambe was the last Netherlands entrant in 2025
The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to take part.
The Netherlands and four other countries boycotted this year's event, after Dutch network Avrotros pulled out.
Avrotros said it would also not take part next year, but NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, stepped in and pledged last month that the country would return in 2027 .
However, NPO's media director Jurre Bosman said on Tuesday that "Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division", and NPO "has decided to forgo participation in 2027".
NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.
"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.
"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.
"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."
NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.
Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".
Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.
"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.
"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."
Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".
The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all bocotted the 2026 contest over Israel's participation, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.
Eurovision organisers have announced a number of changes in an attempt to address the divisions, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition, and changes to the voting.
As well as the Netherlands, Ireland will also not take part in 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.
The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.
Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year with the dance track Bangaranga.

U.S. Treasury yields: Federal Reserve's monetary policy meeting begins
A trader works at the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 21, 2026.
U.S. Treasury yields moved higher on Tuesday as the Federal Reserve's two-day monetary policy meeting kicked off and investors digested a spate of economic data releases.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield rose more than 1 basis point to 5.003%, as did the 30-year Treasury bond to 5.316%. The 2-year Treasury note yield was up 3 basis points at 4.741%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
The Fed was set to begin its two-day monetary policy meeting on Tuesday, with the central bank's latest interest rate decision due on Wednesday.
Traders are widely expecting policymakers to keep the interest rate unchanged at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, but will look for clues as to whether the Fed will hike interest rates again before the end of the year. Fed funds futures trading is now pricing in a roughly 90% chance that the Fed will hold rates steady, according to the CME FedWatch Tool .
Investors will also parse Chairman Kevin Warsh's statement at the press conference following the decision for potential insights on future monetary policy decisions.
Those on Wall Street on Tuesday assessed the latest reading on durable goods orders , which increased 1.8% in September. That was slightly above the 1.7% rise that economists polled by Dow Jones expected.
Traders also reacted to fresh data on consumer confidence and new home sales. In September, new home sales stood at 676,000, marking a 0.6% fall from August but coming in above the 653,000 Dow Jones consensus estimate. Meanwhile, consumer confidence in October rose to 91.7, beating the 81.0 that was estimated.
The latest publication of the personal consumption expenditures index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, is due on Thursday.

The upcoming decision will provide further information about the central bank's assessment of inflation and the potential direction of monetary policy.

Developments affecting the conflict are relevant to energy markets, where oil prices have continued to fluctuate despite the renewed diplomatic activity.

items.title: The Ballon d’Or has a narrow definition of footballing greatness
items.summary: Celebrity, bias towards players in attack and European dominance undermine football’s most prestigious individual award.
items.content:
British-Nigerian journalist, broadcaster and lawyer, covering international football and its politics.
Share The Ballon d’Or has a narrow definition of footballing greatness on social media
England and Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane reacts after receiving the Ballon d'Or award for the best male footballer during the 2026 Ballon d'Or France Football award ceremony at the Palladium Theatre in London on October 26, 2026 [AFP]
The Ballon d’Or is football’s most prestigious individual honour. On Monday, Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane became the first Englishman to win it since Michael Owen in 2001. But his victory also raises a fundamental question about the award: How can individual excellence be fairly assessed in a team sport?
For much of the past two decades, that question has been overshadowed by the extraordinary rivalry between Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. From 2008 to 2017, one or the other won the Ballon d’Or every year, turning the annual award into a contest between the two superstars. Messi eventually accumulated a record eight trophies and Ronaldo five, together accounting for 13 of the 17 awards presented between 2008 and 2025.
Their rivalry generated unprecedented excitement around an award first presented in 1956, when England’s “wizard of the dribble”, Sir Stanley Matthews, became its inaugural winner. But it also pushed several important questions into the background. Has the growing commercialisation of the Ballon d’Or distracted from its purpose? Why does it overwhelmingly reward attacking players? And why does a supposedly global award remain so heavily focused on European football?
The commercialisation of the Ballon d’Or reflects the transformation of football into a global entertainment industry, in which individual players have become brands in their own right.
“The whole dynamic of the Ballon d’Or has changed because the dynamic of the sports and entertainment industry has changed with the way individual athletes are marketed,” Steve Martin, founding partner of MSQ Sport + Entertainment, formerly of M&C Saatchi, told The Athletic.
“They’ve found a way as an individual athlete or player to build their own profile and their own fanbase, as opposed to relying on their clubs. They control their own destiny, and they market themselves.”
Former Switzerland defender Ramon Vega has been more critical of this development. “The commercialisation and monetisation of this award is not taking it in the right direction,” he told the writer.
The Ballon d’Or has undoubtedly become a bigger spectacle, but the attention surrounding the award should not obscure the question of what constitutes individual excellence. And commercialisation is not its only problem. The award has also long favoured players in attack over those in other positions.
A goalkeeper’s or defender’s performance is as important as that of midfielders and strikers, in a sport where a team is supposed to be as great as the sum of its parts. Yet Russia’s Lev Yashin remains the only goalkeeper to have won the award, in 1963, while Italy’s Fabio Cannavaro was the last defender to do so, in 2006, after captaining his country to World Cup victory. Germany’s Franz Beckenbauer and Matthias Sammer were among the few other defenders to have received the honour.
“Goalkeepers and defenders are also part of the spectacle. Attackers don’t just play amongst themselves,” Cannavaro told France Football after winning the award in 2006. “If a goalkeeper has saved 15 or so matches in a year, it’s only fair to highlight him.”
But the Italian’s observations have done little to change the pervasive bias of voters for the award, as strikers and midfielders on the European club and national team stage remain the yardstick for measuring global excellence.
That focus on European football points to another longstanding weakness of the Ballon d’Or: Its failure to adequately recognise outstanding players from elsewhere in the world.
For nearly four decades after the award was established, only European players were eligible to win it. This was a great injustice to exceptional footballers from other continents, even those competing in Europe’s leading leagues. The late Diego Maradona was perhaps the most notable victim of this exclusion.
The restriction was finally lifted in 1995, allowing players of any nationality at European clubs to compete for the prize. It took another 12 years, until 2007, for the award to be opened to players competing anywhere in the world.
It could be argued that when the award began, the club and national team game outside Europe was beyond the close observation and expert knowledge of the Ballon d’Or selectors. But that argument no longer holds water. Knowledge of the global game has grown exponentially, yet recognition of excellence beyond Europe’s leading competitions remains limited.
When Liberia’s George Weah became the first non-European player to win the Ballon d’Or in 1995, following outstanding performances for Paris Saint-Germain and AC Milan, his victory was expected to open the door for exceptional players from parts of the footballing world that had long been denied recognition.
But 31 years on, the former president of Liberia remains the only person outside Europe and South America to have won it.
“When I started playing football, I never thought I would ever win the Ballon d’Or and emerge as the best player in the world. I just had a passion for the game and I worked hard. Every day. I would rather train than eat or sleep,” Weah told the writer in Monrovia.
“I am surprised that no other African player has won the award since I did so. I think there have been others that deserve to win. But it is down to those who select the winners.”
Cameroon’s Samuel Eto’o, the former Barcelona and Inter striker, now president of his country’s football federation, is one person with a right to feel aggrieved that he didn’t win the award before retiring in 2019.
“It’s difficult to understand how Samuel Eto’o never won the Ballon d’Or with the impressive career he had,” Jose Mourinho, who managed Eto’o at Inter, said in a 2019 interview with Cameroon Radio.
“He played in three Champions League finals, winning two with Barcelona and scoring in both finals. He also won one Champions League at Inter and won many league titles. He was the best striker in the world for several years, and I think he deserved a Ballon d’Or, but these are things out of our control.”
Eto’o’s omission, like Weah’s continued status as the only African winner, raises questions about how the award’s selectors and voters assess the achievements of players from outside football’s traditional European and South American powerhouses.
The Ballon d’Or already has an international voting panel, with journalists from 100 countries selecting the winner from a shortlist of 30 players. But geographical representation among voters does not necessarily translate into recognition of the world’s footballing talent.
France Football, the award’s organisers, should ensure that the process of selecting nominees and winners draws on a genuinely global understanding of the game and gives due recognition to exceptional players, regardless of nationality or where they compete.
The award must also address its other shortcomings. Football is a team sport in which goalkeepers, defenders, midfielders and strikers all contribute to success, and individual recognition should reflect that. Nor should the growing commercial appeal of the Ballon d’Or distract from the footballing achievements it was created to honour.
The Ballon d’Or should be a celebration of individual excellence across all positions and all continents, not an award dominated by football’s biggest stars and Europe’s leading competitions. Only then can it truly claim to recognise the best footballer in the world.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
Why the US government is banning Chinese robots – video explainer
US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China , citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum , an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

Is a Stock Market Crash Coming? What History Says a $10,000 Investment in an S&P 500 ETF Could Be Worth at the End of 2027.
Investors have been increasingly worried that an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble is forming and that it could soon burst, sending stocks plummeting. In such a scenario, a $10,000 investment in an S&P 500 exchange-traded fund (ETF) , such as the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO), could be much lower at the end of 2027.
Based on past bear markets, that could result in a 30% loss, and your $10,000 investment would be worth only around $7,000 at year-end 2027. However, that is not the only potential scenario, as we are entering what is also historically a strong period for stocks.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
While the average bull market since 1942 has lasted over four years, the average bear market has lasted just over 11 months. Meanwhile, the average cumulative loss during these bear markets has been 31.7%, according to First Trust and Bloomberg data.
The current AI-driven market has been most often compared to the dot-com boom and subsequent crash. That bear market lasted about one and a half years and saw the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) fall nearly 37%. There are some key differences between these two markets, however.
One is that the S&P 500 today is actually much more heavily weighted toward the companies leading the AI boom. At the end of 1999, before the market burst, the S&P 500 was still very diversified, with Walmart , General Electric, ExxonMobil , Citigroup , and Home Depot among the index's top 10 largest holdings. Today, 40% of the S&P weighting is made up of tech stocks , and every one of its top 10 holdings is an AI stock. That could potentially mean a much harsher pullback than the S&P saw in 2000.
However, balancing that out is that, from a valuation perspective, tech stocks are trading at a much lower valuation today than before the dot-com crash. According to Reuters, the technology sector was valued as high as 48 times the next 12 months' earnings estimates during the dot-com boom. Today, the technology sector trades at a forward P/E of around 19 times. Thus, while the S&P 500 has more tech exposure, it's also starting from a less frothy position. In fact, the S&P 500's PEG ratio -- the trailing P/E ratio divided by the expected earnings growth rate -- is the lowest it's been in more than 30 years, at around 0.7, according to Yardeni Research. This is only the fifth time it's dropped below 1 since at least 1995, and well below its 1.3 average.
Another big difference between these two technological innovation periods is the companies doing the spending and the paybacks on these investments. The internet boom was mainly funded by large telecom and cable companies that were building out broadband networks. These were long-term assets, but with relatively slow payback periods.
The AI boom, meanwhile, is being fueled by megacap tech companies. Cloud computing companies are doing the bulk of the spending and generally see quick paybacks. However, the actual assets depreciate much more quickly with around a five- to six-year replacement cycle, creating a permanent AI spending treadmill. As long as end-user demand and token monetization outpace depreciation, the AI flywheel will continue. However, the risk is that if revenue growth starts to slow, the hardware refresh cycle does not, leading to a big squeeze in margins.
With AI spending looking set to continue to boom over at least the next few years, a market crash next year likely isn't in the cards, in my view. Meanwhile, the market is entering what is historically a very strong period for stocks.
Since 1938, the S&P 500 has risen 95% of the time over the next 12 months following midterm elections. Meanwhile, the index has generated a 14.5% average return from November to November of the following year since 1950. In this scenario, your $10,000 investment in an S&P 500 ETF would be worth nearly $11,500.
Ultimately, trying to predict where the market is headed and when a pullback may occur is a losing bet. While I think the bull market will continue, the best move is to continue to dollar-cost average into an ETF like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF in both good markets and bad. This is what eventually helps you build long-term wealth.

items.title: Co-ordinated cattle raids kill at least 72 people in South Sudan
items.summary: The cycle of revenge attacks continue as the country heads towards its first  election since independence.
items.content:
Image caption, Cattle are a main source of wealth and pride for many communities in South Sudan
At least 72 people have been killed during cattle raids in South Sudan's northern Warrap state, according to the regional government.
An unspecified number of cattle were taken and homes burnt during what was a "co-ordinated attack" on Monday involving two communities in Tonj North county, the state authorities said.
Such deadly violence is often part of a cycle of revenge attacks as cattle are a main source of wealth and pride for many communities and are also important as young men need them as dowries to get married.
Clashes over territory are also common across the country as it prepares to hold its first election since its independence in 2011 - delayed because of a brutal civil war.
The clashes occurred near the border of Warrap and Unity states in the area of Akop Payam, with some members from Lou Ariik community said to have attacked those from Apuk Padoch community.
William Wol Mayom Bol, Warrap state's information minister, said they followed deadly violence last Friday that claimed eight lives.
The state governor, Angelo Ngot Mayar, sent his condolences to bereaved families and directed security agencies to evacuate the wounded.
He said efforts were under way recover the cattle and find those behind the assault.
The state has also appealed to humanitarian partners to support vulnerable women, children and elderly left without food, shelter and medicine.
In August, at least 60 people were killed and 50 injured in an attack in the same area of Warrap state, according to Acled, the non-profit conflict monitoring group.
A similar attack in March led to 58 deaths and 71 injuries.
Last year, a six-month state of emergency was declared in Warrup in efforts to quell the increasing violence.
The UN has also voiced its concerns about the situation in South Sudan as the world's youngest country heads towards presidential elections due to be held in December .
The poll was initially delayed by the civil war, which ended in 2018 with a fragile peace deal signed between President Salva Kiir and his deputy Riek Machar.
However tensions between the leaders led to further delays: Machar was sacked as vice-president and arrested earlier last year and charged with murder, treason and crimes against humanity, which he denies.
He has been under house arrest in the capital, Juba, since March last year as fighting persists in some areas of the country.
Preparations for the elections have lagged and human rights groups have raised questions over whether the country can complete key things like voter registration and security arrangements before the vote.

AMD and Nvidia Split the AI Chip Market. 1 Stock Is Far Cheaper Today.
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) are two of the biggest names in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market. Their graphics processing units (GPUs) are the most popular options, and each is growing rapidly. However, from an investment standpoint, they are fundamentally different, especially when price tags are considered.
Nvidia is far cheaper than AMD, and this is something that investors can't ignore. I think that makes Nvidia the superior buy, but is there more to this picture? Let's take a look.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Image source: The Motley Fool. Nvidia is defying the law of large numbers
Nvidia and AMD both make GPUs, which are general purpose computing units that can excel in just about any situation. This makes them the workhorse of the AI computing landscape, even as other custom AI alternatives grow more popular. Those custom chips are only meant to run one type of workload and will never fully replace GPUs.
In the early days of the AI arms race, Nvidia's products were far superior, which allowed it to capture an early lead. While AMD has improved its game, Nvidia's early lead has been tough to overcome. However, the law of large numbers suggests that the larger a company gets, the harder it is to grow. Therefore, if AMD is smaller, then it should be able to grow faster than Nvidia. If everything else is equal, a faster-growing stock will lead to better long-term returns, which would push AMD ahead of Nvidia as an investment option. The problem is, it isn't happening.
Nvidia is far larger than AMD. Nvidia's data center division (the sector most exposed to AI) saw revenue of $89 billion during the second quarter of its fiscal year (FY) 2027 (ended July 26). AMD's Q2 (which ended on June 30) saw revenue of $6.7 billion. The company's financial calendars are about one month apart, so this isn't a perfect comparison, but it's the best that investors can do. With AMD's data center division being more than 10 times smaller than Nvidia, it should have no problem growing faster, but Nvidia's growth in Q2 was 117% versus AMD's 107%.
While both companies are each delivering strong results, Nvidia is clearly growing faster despite its much larger size. But there's more to this analysis.
AMD and Nvidia also have non-data-center segments. However, Nvidia's other businesses are far smaller, and data center revenue accounts for the majority of Nvidia's $96.2 billion total. AMD's Q2 revenue was $11.5 billion, so other divisions make up a far higher percentage of its revenue. The problem is that these product lines aren't growing nearly as fast, so AMD's overall growth rate significantly lags Nvidia's.
AMD Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts. With this kind of growth disparity, you'd expect Nvidia to have a premium valuation relative to AMD, as it is growing far faster. But that's not the case.
Because these two are expected to grow rapidly over the next few quarters, I think valuing them based on forward earnings makes a lot of sense. From this perspective, AMD is basically three times more expensive than Nvidia.
AMD PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts. That's a huge gap that doesn't seem logical, but that's how the market is pricing these two stocks. I think this is a huge mistake, and eventually it will correct itself so that these two stocks trade at roughly the same valuation. Whether that's caused by an AMD sell-off or an Nvidia rise is uncertain, but I'm confident that Nvidia will be the far better stock to own over the next few years. Its broad exposure to the AI arms race will boost the stock over the next few years, leading it to outperform AMD over the long term.

items.content:
New poll shows Democrats have midterm edge, with caution signs Democrats hold significant advantages going into Election Day, according to a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll. But lagging enthusiasm among key groups is just one indicator that gains may not come easy.
Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows warning signs for just how many
Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows warning signs for just how many
< iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6017479/nx-s1-9979951" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
A member of the League of Women Voters of Greater Cleveland helps hold the flag during the national anthem before a basketball game on Oct. 26, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio.
📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the  NPR App
Democrats retain significant midterm electoral advantages, with key data pointing to them being the favorites to win control of the U.S. House. But, there are indications of why a potential wave could be limited, a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds.
The poll also sheds light on the issues driving voters across the ideological spectrum. The cost of living continues to be top of mind overall with a third of people saying they've experienced financial hardship in the past year and 4 in 10 saying their personal finances have gotten worse.
"The economy is at the top of my list right now," said Shun Maurice, a 47-year-old from Arizona who participated in the poll. He's an independent who leans toward Democrats and said high food and gas prices are a strain.
"They're too expensive for everybody, no matter who you voted for," he said. "They're just too expensive for the American people in general, and I don't like that."
Preserving democracy also continues to resonate with Democrats and independents, while immigration is the biggest concern for self-described MAGA supporters.
The poll of 1,289 registered voters was conducted Oct. 19-20. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points.
Most don't think Trump is doing a good job and don't like him
This was the first survey this cycle that Marist applied a likely voter screen, and on multiple questions, likely voters were — within the margin of error — slightly less likely than registered voters to disapprove of the president. Likely voters overall were also slightly less likely to want Democrats to run Congress.
Likely voters are something of a special sauce in polling. Survey researchers apply various metrics — like levels of enthusiasm, past voting history and how important voting is to different respondents — to try to identify the subsample of people who are most likely to vote.
Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections
In this survey, just 38% of registered voters approved of the job President Trump is doing, with 61% disapproving (-23). Likely voters gave him a 40% to 59% rating (-19), still not very good, but even a slight margin can make a difference in how significant the gains either party might make in the election are.
That said, an equal share — 53% — of registered and likely voters said they "strongly disapprove" of the job Trump is doing, tied with last month as the highest ever in the poll.
Trump's favorability rating is even lower — just 37% of likely voters have a favorable impression of Trump, while 59% have a negative one.
Democrats retain the edge on the congressional ballot
Democrats also had a strong advantage on which party's candidate people said they are more likely to vote for in their district if the election were held today, known as the generic congressional ballot. Among registered voters, it was a 10-point advantage. With likely voters, it was 8 points, still indicative of Democratic gains.
When Democrats have had that kind of lead on the congressional ballot, they have historically done very well. On average, it was +7 in 2018 and +12 in 2006. In both years, Democrats won the House with at least 30 seats flipped.
But that was before the 2020 Census and ensuing regular redistricting — and the rare, mid-decade redistricting in the last year and a half after Trump asked Republican states to redraw their maps to potentially give Republicans more seats. Though Democrats followed suit, both redistricting periods have tilted congressional seats in Republicans' direction and given them a relative advantage nationally.
Perhaps because of some of those structural disadvantages and past performance, there is a notable degree of nervousness among Democrats.
While 98% of Democratic likely voters said they would vote for a Democrat, just 81% thought the Democrat would win, a 17-point difference. Republicans were only 10 points less likely to believe their candidate would win. Notably, among independents, a higher share thought the Democratic candidate would win.
Working in Democrats' favor — and against incumbents: 55% of likely voters said it's more important in this election to vote for candidates with new ideas who will bring about change. (It was a tick higher with registered voters at 57%.)
Chris Agan, a 43-year-old Democrat in Tyler, Texas, who participated in the survey, never saw himself as an impassioned midterm voter, until this year.
"This year is different. This year, it feels like every opportunity to vote is a referendum against the party in power," said Agan, who's backing Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in the race for U.S. Senate.
"We've been seeing a very slow decline in the standard of living in this state, and it's becoming apparently evident to more people at this time," he added. "I think Talarico embodies that realization that there needs to be change."
Ohio could decide control of the Senate. Its rural voters might decide the winner
In Arkansas, Democrats see an opening at the edge of the competitive midterms map
Double the percentage of likely voters also said their vote would be one against Trump (44%) as opposed to one for him (21%). In the 2024 presidential election, 55% of those who voted for Trump said their vote was for their candidate, according to exit polls .
Trump is not on the ballot, but he has asked voters to "pretend" he is.
Though Trump's unpopularity poses challenges for Republicans, it may not directly translate to more votes for Democrats. Some swing voters don't like the lurch in some corners of the Democratic Party toward democratic socialism.
Matthew Schroder is a 38-year-old independent living in Charlotte, N.C., who was part of the poll. He backed Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024. Now, he says that while he's unhappy with Trump's job performance, it isn't what's driving his vote this year.
"What I have seen on the left-hand side is a little bit more of an embrace of democratic socialism, which I just oppose completely," said Schroder, who's supporting Republican Michael Whatley over Democrat Roy Cooper in the state's closely watched race for U.S. Senate.
"I know Roy Cooper is considered a moderate, but the fact that the Democratic Party is even letting some of these voices be heard a little bit more … is not something I'm interested in in the least," he added. "It's not a vote of 'yes for Trump' as much as a vote of, Democrats need to completely reject [democratic socialism] and go a completely different direction."
Democrats also have the enthusiasm advantage, but there are some caution flags, too
Democratic likely voters are 10 points more likely to say they are "very enthusiastic" about voting (71% vs. 61%). That's actually wider than the difference between Democratic and Republican registered voters in the poll.
The caution for Democrats, though, is that several of their key pillar groups are not very enthusiastic to vote, and Republicans have closed the gap on who is following the election "very closely."
Just 42% of likely voters under 45, 53% of non-white voters and 56% of white women with college degrees said they are "very enthusiastic" to vote. All of those groups disapproved of the job Trump is doing.
Compare that to pro-Trump groups — MAGA voters (68%), white women without degrees (66%) and white evangelical voters (61%).
For independents, 48% report being very enthusiastic to vote.
Republicans are spending millions and still may not win districts drawn to favor them
Traditionally, younger, as well as Black and Latino voters turn out at disproportionately lower rates in midterm elections. But with the realignment under Trump, more white, college-educated voters are voting Democratic and, as a group, they turn out at the highest rates.
When it comes to paying close attention, last month just 34% of registered Republicans said they're following the election very closely, compared to 42% of Democrats.
Now, they're even – 46% of Democrats and 45% of Republicans said they're paying very close attention. When it comes to likely voters, there's no difference either – 51% of Democrats to 50% of Republicans.
On the positive side for Democrats: those who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 are 15 points more likely than Trump 2024 voters to say they are very enthusiastic. And Democrats overall have an 8-point advantage over Republicans when it comes to who cares a "great deal" about who controls Congress.
Most are confident elections will be fair and accurate, but Republicans lag
Three-quarters of likely voters are confident that their state and local governments will run a fair and accurate election.
That includes solid majorities of Democrats (88%), Republicans (68%) and independents (75%), but Republicans were 20 points less likely than Democrats to think they would be run well. MAGA supporters were almost 30 points less likely.
The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections
Large majorities also said their preferred candidate should accept the results of the election. That included 70% of Republicans, but again, they were 20 points less likely than Democrats to say they should accept the results. A quarter of Republicans said their candidate should probably or definitely challenge the results.
There was also a sharp divide between those who identified as democratic socialists and MAGA supporters — 86% of democratic socialists but only 65% of MAGA supporters said their preferred candidate should accept the result. MAGA supporters were twice as likely to say they should challenge.
Personal finances: 38% said their personal finances have gotten worse in the past year, though 44% said they've stayed about the same. Younger generations are experiencing more financial insecurity than older ones. And they're more likely to have moved, changed jobs or lost one in the past year.
AI continues to face an uphill public-opinion challenge: 6-in-10 said the construction of new data centers will mostly have a negative impact on the country, though majorities of Republicans and MAGA supporters said it would be a net-positive. An even higher percentage (66%) said they oppose construction of a data center in their community. Republicans are split on this, but Democrats and independents overwhelmingly oppose them. The intensity of opposition is pretty high, as well, with 41% saying they strongly oppose them.
Immigration: 61% said immigrants should have a way to stay in the country legally if they meet certain requirements. Two-thirds of Republicans, though, said they should be required to leave.
Government continues to be a sharp dividing line: 57% said government is almost always wasteful and inefficient. That included majorities of Republicans and independents. Almost 6 in 10 Democrats, though, said government often does a better job than people give it credit for. That also included 59% of democratic socialists.
People are split on guns: 48% said it's more important to pass stricter gun-control laws, while 46% said protecting the right of Americans to own guns was the higher priority. While independents were largely split, roughly 9 in 10 Democrats said gun control and 85% of Republicans said gun rights.
Theoretical belief in equality: People were asked which comes closer to their view – An ideal society needs equality for all groups or one that needs some groups to be on top and others to be on the bottom – 70% said equality, though Republicans were largely split. Meanwhile, this is a core pillar for democratic socialists, as 97% of them surveyed said equality.
Methodology: This NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll was conducted from Oct. 19-20 and surveyed a national sample of 1,289 registered voters. They were reached through a multi-mode design: by phone, text or online. To create a likely voter sample, Marist applied a likely voter weight to all registered voters. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points. That means results fall within a range of roughly eight points – about four points lower or higher.
